title: Returning to the Tin Palace and the West End in 1979
summary: He found audiences wanting romantic, basic music; he played the Tin Palace with John Hicks, Walter Booker and Jimmy Cobb and the West End, where old friends like Beverly Peer came.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: All right, now, these last few months you've come up a number of times and played at the Tin Palace, at the West End, and now at the Vanguard. I wonder, in terms of being in New York these past few months, what changes you notice from the time that you were here before.

Well, what I noticed this time was that, you know, the wheel always turns, the wheel never stops turning, but people want to go back to basic things and they want to go back to soul and people, I mean they want a little more romantic music, mainly, that's what they want. They want something that they can actually feel, outside of electronics and all of these things. But they want something that they can feel and the stimulus for that, I can feel it, you know. And when I came to the Tin Palace the first time in October (sic), was that people wanted to hear, you know, some tradition of the people who been in this life all their life. And the warm reception that I received from musicians that I been knowin' through the years, it encouraged me. And, of course, the trio that I had there: Walter Booker on bass and Jimmy Cobbs (sic) on drums and John Hicks on piano, they had the right attitude. Of course Jimmy Cobbs is older, but John Hicks and Walter Booker are young, but they have the right mental attitude of projecting a happiness on stage. And then I noticed, which was a very warm thing, that people I been knowin' for years, they came by. The owners there said. 'It's like

New Year's Eve," you know, they'd never seen so many musicians in the Tin Palace. But most of these people they were, you know, my peers or they came up under me and it was like a festive thing and it was very heart warming. Then when I went up to the West End which is an establishment that's been there for many years, everybody was very warm and I saw some old friends. I saw Beverly Peer, who's with Bobby Short...
How far do you and Beverly go back, you were in the same...?

We went to the...we were with Sabby Lewis and then he went to Boston Conservatory with me, you know. We did courses. And he came by. Several people came. Lou Donaldson came by and Tommy Turrentine. A lot of people came by and that was a nice, nice job. And I noticed that the people want to hear those old things. And things that are really jazz classics, they wanted to hear that. And we had a good time. Then when I went back to the Tin Palace, for New Year's Eve, it was really wonderful because I've played so many

New Year's Eves in New York City on a steady job and this New Year's Eve at the Tin Palace, I'm sure that they...Walter Booker told me he's never had a New Year's Eve like that. What I did was use all of my experiences of all the New Year's Eves I've played and everybody had a wonderful time so I feel good about coming back to New York. Yeah.
